purpose: Independent practice of B2.4 (modelling and solving story problems with totals to 50). Captures formative evidence on the build-draw-write pipeline.
student_learning_goal: I can act out, draw, and write an equation for an addition or subtraction story problem with numbers up to 50.

header.student_learning_goal_banner: I can act out, draw, and write an equation for an addition or subtraction story problem with numbers up to 50.
header.character_watermark: Plus the Pup and Minnie the Mouse together in the top-right corner. Small (~1.5in tall combined).

parts.student_instructions: Sketch a tape diagram with both parts labelled. Write the addition equation. Solve and circle the total.
parts.visual_layout: Top of the page. Two story-problem boxes side by side. Each box has the story text on top and a blank tape-diagram frame plus equation lines below.

How many buttons does Lila have now?' Box B story: 'Plus had 18 dog treats. Minnie gave him 12 more. How many treats does Plus have now?' Below each story: a blank rectangle (tape diagram frame, ~3in × 0.7in) with a 'Total = ___' label above it; an equation line '___ + ___ = ___'.
image_placeholders.placement: Top of the page; two story boxes side by side.
image_placeholders.text_image_alignment_check: Image WS04_P1_TWO_CHANGE_ADD: keywords (story, tape-diagram, equation) name what the boxes ask for.

parts.answer_key: Box A: tape diagram with parts 14 and 9, total 23. Equation 14+9=23. Lila has 23 buttons. Box B: tape diagram with parts 18 and 12, total 30. Equation 18+12=30. Plus has 30 treats.

parts.student_instructions: Show the take-from on a tape diagram. Write the subtraction equation. Solve and circle what is left.
parts.visual_layout: Upper-middle of the page. Two story-problem boxes side by side. Same format as Part 1 but with subtraction stories.

image_placeholders.description: Two story-problem boxes in B&W line-art, side by side, each ~3.5in × 3in. Box A story: 'Otto had 16 marbles. He lost 7 of them under the couch. How many marbles does Otto have now?' Box B story: 'Plus had 25 dog treats. He gave 13 to Scoot. How many treats does Plus have left?' Below each story: a blank tape-diagram frame and an equation line '___ - ___ = ___'.
image_placeholders.placement: Upper-middle; two story boxes side by side.
image_placeholders.text_image_alignment_check: Image WS04_P2_TWO_CHANGE_TAKE: keywords (story, tape-diagram, subtraction) name what the boxes ask for.

parts.answer_key: Box A: tape diagram with parts 7 (lost) and 9 (kept), total 16. Equation 16-7=9. Otto has 9 marbles. Box B: tape diagram with parts 13 (given) and 12 (left), total 25. Equation 25-13=12. Plus has 12 treats.

parts.student_instructions: Sketch the part-part-whole on a tape diagram. Write your equation. Solve and circle the answer.
parts.visual_layout: Middle-lower of the page. Two story-problem boxes side by side. Same tape-diagram-and-equation format.

parts.student_instructions: Write your own change-take-from story problem. Draw a tape diagram. Write the equation. Solve.
parts.visual_layout: Bottom of the page. A blank box (~7in × 4in) for the child to write a story, draw a tape diagram, write the equation, and solve.

parts.answer_key: Open. Accept any plausible change-take-from story. Look for: (a) the story has a clear starting amount, a clear amount taken away, and a clear question; (b) the tape diagram has both parts labeled; (c) the equation matches the story (subtraction); (d) the answer is correctly computed.

early_finisher_prompt: If you finish, write a SECOND story problem on the back of the page — this time a part-part-whole story.
teacher_notes: Lesson 4 consolidation. Hand out at the end of the Action phase. Watch for: (a) children who write the equation and answer but skip the tape diagram — flag for diagram-as-thinking-tool reteach; (b) children who draw a single rectangle with the answer inside (no parts) — same flag; (c) Part 4 children who write a story but not in the correct change-take-from structure (e.g., they write a part-part-whole story instead) — coaching opportunity for problem-type identification. Use Parts 1-3 as evidence for the formative tracker; Part 4 as evidence for child-generated reasoning.
